The Marianas Trench pressure is approximately 1,086 atm (approx. 1100 atm), and the peak temperature is around 4°C. For Freon-12 (R-12), the critical pressure is only about 41 atm. Since the ambient pressure (1100 atm) is vastly higher than the critical pressure, the refrigerant will be compressed into a supercritical fluid, not a liquid. The density of a supercritical fluid at these conditions (1100 atm, 4°C) would be much higher than the estimated 1.5 g/cm³ (likely exceeding 2.0 g/cm³ or more depending on the specific P-V-T equation of state used), leading to a significantly smaller volume than the calculated 208 mL. Furthermore, the density of a liquid at 4°C is typically higher than at 0°C (around 1.56 g/cm³ for R-12), so even the liquid approximation was slightly off. The primary error is the failure to account for the supercritical state, which renders the simple liquid density approximation invalid for this specific high-pressure scenario.
